title: Across Arctic America: Narrative of the Fifth Thule Expedition
author: Knud Rasmussen (reporting Igjugarjuk, Kinalik, Aua)
edition_cited: New York and London: G. P. Putnam's Sons, 1927; archive.org scan acrossarcticamer006641mbp (OCR text, some garbling)
tradition: Inuit (Caribou Inuit of the Barren Grounds; Iglulik) angakkuq shamanism
locator_hints: Chapter 'A Nomad's Life', printed pp. 81-86 (file lines c. 3796-3990): Igjugarjuk's doctrine ('All true wisdom is only to be learned far from the dwellings of men') and his thirty-day initiation in a tiny snow hut; Kinalik's and Aggjartoq's ordeals

Chapter 'Faith out of Fear', printed pp. 126-127 (file lines c. 5510-5550): Iglulik novitiate and Aua: 'a great glow as of intense light pervaded all his being (this is a recurrent feature in the process)'
summary: Rasmussen's popular narrative of the expedition, useful as a second witness beside the Iglulik report. For the Iglulik it condenses Aua's account: ordinary instruction failed, then 'without knowing how' a glow as of intense light pervaded his whole being, with inexpressible joy and song; Rasmussen adds that this glow is 'a recurrent feature in the process'. For the Caribou Inuit it gives Igjugarjuk's own training in detail: carried in midwinter to a snow hut barely large enough to sit cross-legged, no food or drink, told to think only of the Great Spirit and the helper to come; water after five days, a little meat after fifteen more, thirty days in all, then five months of strict diet and continence, the fast repeated. He reports a helping spirit arriving in sleep; no light is mentioned in his case.
why_relevant: Gives the fullest procedure (solitude, cold, fasting, single-pointed thought, durations) attached to the Inuit tradition of shamanic light, and a contrast case where the same ordeal is reported without light.
